note.question: How does a payer's telehealth reimbursement rate affect a provider's division of capacity between office and virtual care, strategic patients' channel choices, duplicate visits, and overall acute-care access?
note.overview: The paper nests a strategic patient queueing equilibrium inside sequential reimbursement and provider-capacity decisions, so equilibrium analysis is central rather than incidental.

coverage.note: The existing independently audited model map was decomposed into Mini-style components and linked back to the page-preserving source extraction.

inputs: Patients make symmetric choices using equilibrium waiting-time expectations

A telehealth visit may generate a duplicate office visit with publicly known probability q

Provider chooses telehealth capacity commitment theta

The provider maximizes reimbursement revenue rather than patient access or social welfare
The main large-market model uses stationary Markovian queueing primitives; the paper also studies a small-market variant and operational extensions

models.method: Stationary queueing analysis and patient indifference conditions characterize the downstream symmetric equilibrium; regime thresholds and concavity then solve the provider response and payer policy by backward induction.

sources.quote: Unlike in our main model, in the second stage of the game, rather than each provider offering one or both channels, we consider the case where the providers may specialize—that is, one provider offers service exclu­ sively via telehealth, and the other provider exclusively via the office, in which case duplicate visits resulting from the telehealth provider’s panel are referred to the office of the other provider.

components.label: subgame-perfect Stackelberg equilibrium with a symmetric patient queueing Nash equilibrium
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is subgame-perfect Stackelberg equilibrium with a symmetric patient queueing Nash equilibrium. The patient subgame is partitioned into office-only, telehealth-only, both-channel, and balking regimes; provider and payer choices are then solved backward using those equilibrium regimes.
